summary: This final issue of South Korean Interim Government Activities, prepared by the National Economic Board Statistics Division, covers July-August 1948 and the transition on 15 August 1948 from US Army Military Government to the Republic of Korea under President Rhee Syngman. It opens with a summation of three years of occupation, citing food self-sufficiency prospects, fertilizer imports, farmland sales, a narrowing trade deficit and vested property returned to Korean management. Regular sections report prices (wholesale index 184 percent of 1947), industrial output under reduced power after the 14 May North Korean cutoff, labor, transport, communications, finance with a 22,000 million won overdraft, politics, police, and social fields. Historians will find refugee and population statistics, trade figures, the Constitution and cabinet formation, and retrospective accounts of each department.
highlights: The Republic of Korea was proclaimed on 15 August 1948 under President Rhee Syngman, and USAMGIK was succeeded by the Civil Affairs Section of USAFIK; MG personnel had fallen to 2,870.
Refugees from the north numbered 185,441 in 1946, 163,235 in 1947 and 86,036 by mid-August 1948; cumulative inbound movement was 2,454,480 against 886,618 outbound.
Wholesale prices rose to 184 percent of the 1947 average in August, up from 171 in July, ending five months of stability, while the SKIG overdraft exceeded 22,000 million won.
After the North Korean power cutoff of 14 May, local generation recovered to 55,600,000 KWH in August from 33,000,000 in April; anthracite output fell from 68,612 tons to 38,887.
Management of 35 vested companies passed to elected Boards of Directors, and the National Land Administration had sold 481,957 acres of farmland, about 85 percent of available farms.
The Assembly elected Rhee Syngman President with 180 votes and approved Lee Bum-suk as Prime Minister 110 to 84 after the Constitution of 12 July.
The 1948 crop was estimated near 6,000,000 metric tons, the highest since 1941, with food self-sufficiency expected by January 1949 and fertilizer imports above 548,000 tons.
Korea competed in the London Olympics under its own flag for the first time, sending 67 athletes and placing 24th with 15 points.

sections.title: Front matter
sections.summary: Cover and front matter of the final SKIG Activities report (No. 34, July-August 1948). Lists Board members under Chairman Wilhelm Anderson, Arthur G. Peterson's Forward on the 15 August 1948 Republic, and the table of contents.

sections.title: Summary
sections.summary: Chairman Wilhelm Anderson reviews three years of occupation: 500,000 tons of imported fertilizer, near food self-sufficiency, the 14 May power cutoff, 85,000 million won of vested property, 481,957 acres sold, and a 22,000 million won overdraft.

sections.title: Part I: Basic Aspects
sections.summary: Covers refugees and population (86,036 refugees from the north to mid-August 1948) and vested property, including 1,119 title claims heard and 35 companies passed to elected boards.

sections.title: Section 1. Population and Foreign Affairs
sections.summary: Refugees from the north totalled 86,036 in 1948 to mid-August, after 185,441 in 1946; inbound movement was 2,454,480 against 886,618 outbound. 151 Turk-Tartars awaited emigration; population estimated at 20.3 million.

sections.title: Section 2. Vested Property
sections.summary: Office of Property Custody prepared handover to the Republic. Claims hearings covered 1,119 cases; Corporate Affairs investigated 5,358 companies and passed 35 to elected boards. Net worth of vested property was about 85,850 million won.

sections.title: Part II: Production and Supply
sections.summary: Covers the 1948 economy: crop near 6,000,000 tons, wholesale prices at 184 percent of 1947, power-limited output, coal losses after 14 May, trade of 3,643 million won imports, and about 118,000 unionists.

sections.title: Section 1. Food and Agriculture
sections.summary: The 1948 crop is estimated near 6,000,000 metric tons, highest since 1941, with self-sufficiency expected by January 1949. Summer grain collection reached 95.8 percent of quota; fertilizer imports passed 548,000 tons; 481,957 acres of farmland sold.

sections.title: Section 2. Prices
sections.summary: Wholesale prices rose to 184 percent of the 1947 average in August, from 171 in July, led by grains, fish, raw cotton and salt. Controlled grain prices rose 1 August; a new urban worker index stood at 179.

sections.title: Section 3. Industrial Production
sections.summary: July-August 1948 output suffered from the power shortage: flour 707 and 1,782 tons, paper mills short of pulp, cement halted, salt hit by rains. Explains why 1947 output looks far below 1940.

sections.title: Section 4. Mining and Minerals
sections.summary: Coal output fell after the 14 May 1948 Soviet power cutoff: anthracite dropped from 68,612 tons in April to 38,887 in July. Bituminous imports from Japan hit a record 104,055 tons in July.

sections.title: Section 5. Allocations and Distribution
sections.summary: National Consumer Goods Office (est. 12 January 1948) processed 1,095 allocations worth 2.18 billion won by 31 August. Salt production reached 68,774 tons by 15 August; barter with North Korea brought 950.9 million won inflow.

sections.title: Section 6. Imports and Exports
sections.summary: Private trade for January-July 1948 was about 3,643 million won imports and 2,763 million exports. Government exports to Japan were $828,457; paper led imports, sea products and straw hats led exports.

sections.title: Section 7. Labor
sections.summary: About 118,000 unionists in some 500 unions, mostly in rightist Tai Han. Wage Stabilization Division formed 25 March 1948; Pusan stevedores sought a 350 won minimum; Tai Han won the Yongwol election with 2,099 votes.

sections.title: Part III: Public Services
sections.summary: Covers transportation, communications, public utilities and public works: record August rail revenue, 37,183 telephones, power deliveries of 55.6 million KWH in August, and flood damage over 2,000 million won.

sections.title: Section 1. Transportation
sections.summary: August transport revenue was the highest since liberation. Rail had 268 operable engines in August with higher freight income; the marine fleet included LSTs and the Rainbow service. Expenditures exceeded income.

sections.title: Section 2. Communications
sections.summary: July communications revenue was the highest since liberation after the June rate increase, while expenditures more than doubled to 196.9 million won. Noted 37,183 telephones, 623 post offices and 11 radio stations.

sections.title: Section 3. Public Utilities
sections.summary: North Korea's 14 May 1948 power cutoff and the Chung Pyung transformer failure caused shortages; deliveries recovered to 56.2 million KWH in July and 55.6 million in August. Giroux Commission reported 23 July.

sections.title: Section 4. Public Works
sections.summary: Summer 1948 brought preparation for transfer to the Korean Government and flood damage exceeding 2,000 million won. The Emergency Water Conservation Board was set up 28 July; road and bridge repairs and subsidy requests noted.

sections.title: Part IV: Finance
sections.summary: Covers government finance (SKIG overdraft of 22,506 million won, F/Y 1948/49 appropriations of 35,264 million won) and private finance (deposits of 43,335 million won).

sections.title: Section 1. Government Finance
sections.summary: Bank of Chosun note issue was about 30,000 million won at end of August; SKIG overdraft 22,506 million. August revenue 2,157 million against expenditure 1,924 million; F/Y 1948/49 appropriations 35,264 million won.

sections.title: Section 2. Non-Government Finance
sections.summary: Private finance through July: cash balances 2,244 million won, deposits 43,335 million (57 percent public), loans outstanding 30,038 million with record June and July lending. Life insurance in force passed 1,067 million won.

sections.title: Part V: Government and Politics
sections.summary: Covers administration, the Constitution and election of Rhee Syngman, legal affairs, police, and inter-zone activities as USAMGIK gave way to the Republic on 15 August 1948.

sections.title: Section 1. Administration
sections.summary: The new government (Tai Han Min Kook) was proclaimed 15 August 1948, ending USAMGIK; the 10 May election drew over 90 percent of 7,730,000 voters. NEB raised rice to 150 won per small mal; MG personnel fell to 2,870.

sections.title: Section 2. Political Developments
sections.summary: Constitution adopted 12 July. The Assembly elected Rhee Syngman President (180 votes) and Lee Si-young Vice-President, and approved Lee Bum-suk as Prime Minister 110 to 84. Moderates split between Kim Koo, Kimm Kiu-sic and the North.

sections.title: Section 3. Legal Affairs
sections.summary: Justice drafted Ordinances Nos. 203-219 and Executive Orders Nos. 24-28. Cheju-do riot trials were movable to Mokpo or Kwangju. Prisoners numbered 22,321 in July; 664 juveniles were in correction houses.

sections.title: Section 4. National Police
sections.summary: Police focused on communist efforts to force signatures for the 25 August North Korean election, with 200 officials held in Taegu. A torture death in Metropolitan Police caused resignations; a fourth attempt on Chang Taik-sang failed 24 July.

sections.title: Section 5. Inter-Zone Activities
sections.summary: North-South mail exchange continued at Tosong with 9 trips in July-August 1948. Commerce Order No. 4 on interzonal barter took effect 2 August; an American soldier was killed at the 38th parallel on 19 July.

sections.title: Part VI: Social
sections.summary: Covers health, education, press, youth, women and culture: 254,664 flood-needy people, school districts created 12 August, Korean National Youth membership of 1,154,821, and Korea's first Olympic entry under its own flag.

sections.title: Section 1. Public Health and Welfare
sections.summary: Floods and typhoons left 254,664 people needy; hog cholera hit five provinces (43,428 hogs). Two smallpox outbreaks were controlled, with about 420,000 vaccinated in Seoul; 28,698 kg of opium returned to Japan.

sections.title: Section 2. Education
sections.summary: Three ordinances effective 12 August 1948 created school districts, nine-member school boards and local school taxation. Teacher workshops reached 7,500 teachers; textbook output was 421,660 copies in July.

sections.title: Section 3. Press and Public Opinion
sections.summary: The press focused on forming the new government: the police-under-Internal Affairs vote (108 to 88), rejection of Lee Yun-yung, approval of Lee Bum-suk as Premier. Table lists 11 leading dailies among 58.

sections.title: Section 4. Korean National Youth, Inc.
sections.summary: Korean National Youth, Inc., chartered 9 October 1945, reached 1,154,821 members by 15 August 1948 and gave over 12,600,000 work-days of labor. Lee Jun-sic succeeded Lee Bum-suk after he became Prime Minister.

sections.title: Section 5. Women's Activities
sections.summary: The new Constitution and Military Government ordinances guarantee women equality. Louise Yim became Minister of Commerce and Industry; the Women's Bureau ran a magazine, classes and the Federation of Women's Clubs.

sections.title: Section 6. Culture
sections.summary: Hangul was reintroduced in schools; the American Language Institute taught English to about 500 students. Korea's first Olympic entry under its own flag at London sent 67 athletes and placed 24th with 15 points.
